name: Nuni, nʋnɩ
confidence_why: one confirmed first-hand source; 4 other works read were silent
catalog_citation: Malgoubri, Pierre. 2011. Recherches dialectologiques et dialectométriques nuni (une langue gurunsi du Burkina Faso). Doctoral dissertation, Leiden University (LOT / Leiden University Repository, hdl:1887/16436). 351 pp.
catalog_locator: §3.1.3 'Les tons', printed p. 54 (PDF p. 67 of 351); saved file (the copy we hold is a symlink to that folder)
catalog_quote: En nʋnɩ, en plus des consonnes et des voyelles qui sont utilisées pour distinguer des mots, la hauteur de la voix est employée à des fins distinctives. Cette variation de la hauteur de la voix permet d’opposer deux (2) mots dont les signifiants sont par ailleurs identiques. Il y a trois tons phonologiques dans la langue: - un ton haut [ ́] - un ton bas [ ̀] - un ton moyen [ ̄] Les mots suivants montrent que la différence de sens est basée sur l’emploi de hauteurs différentes : dí « manger » dì « monter » dī « terrasser » kárá « champ » kārā « cour intérieur » kàrà « étudier » Dans tous les dialectes nʋnɩ, nous trouvons la présence de ces trois différents tons. Nous nous sommes focalisé sur les différences segmentales. Les différences tonales n’ont pas été examinées et décrites. Nous réservons cette description des différences tonales pour nos recherches futures.
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

new_statements.translation: In Nuni, besides the consonants and vowels used to distinguish words, voice pitch is used distinctively. This variation in pitch opposes two words whose signifiers are otherwise identical. There are three phonological tones in the language: a high tone, a low tone, a mid tone [...] dí 'eat', dì 'climb', dī 'knock down' [...] In all Nuni dialects we find these three tones. We focused on segmental differences; tonal differences were not examined or described.
new_statements.citation: Malgoubri, Pierre. 2011. Recherches dialectologiques et dialectométriques nuni (une langue gurunsi du Burkina Faso). Doctoral dissertation, Leiden University.
new_statements.check: confirmed by a second reader, with minor differences

new_statements.rule_in_words: Nuni is a three-tone language (H, M, L) with lexical tone contrasts on monosyllables and disyllables; the only accessible modern description says nothing at all about word stress or accent, so no stress rule can be stated from it.
new_statements.exceptions: None; the author explicitly sets tonal differences among dialects aside for future work.
new_statements.domain_note: Lexical (word-level) tone shown on citation forms; the thesis is a dialectometric study, its phonology chapter is a summary of earlier descriptions plus the author's own data from Léo, Biéha, Bognounou, Cassou, Nébiélanayou, Pouni, Sapouy and Silly. The extracted text renders the vowel ʋ of 'nʋnì' as '√' (font artifact); the quote restores ʋ and the tone diacritics.
new_statements.identity_note: Malgoubri 2011 treats 'nuni' as one language with seven dialects spanning Sissili, Ziro and southern Sanguié provinces; its data include Pouni/Zawara/Silly (his yatìnì dialect), which is the Northern Nuni [nuv] area of the Glottolog page, alongside Léo-area varieties that belong to Southern Nuni [nnw] (Glottolog code for the southern language not verified here). The three-tone statement is asserted for all dialects. Prost 1971/1999 and WALS 'Nuni (Northern)' are based on the Pouni variety (nuv proper).

sources.note: Ch. 3.1 'Les caractéristiques phonologiques' (vowels, consonants, §3.1.3 Les tons, printed p. 54 = PDF p. 67): three phonological tones H/L/M, present in all Nuni dialects; tone differences deliberately left aside. No mention of stress/accent anywhere (a full-text search for stress/accent/intensité/proéminence/tonique: only non-technical uses).
